speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: asked the Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (a) whether the Government assesses that Temasek’s and GIC’s risk-adjusted returns relative to appropriate global benchmarks remain competitive; and (b) how their mandates should evolve to balance capital preservation with the need for higher real returns ahead.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: asked the Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (a) whether the Government is satisfied with the long-term investment performances of GIC, Temasek and MAS when measured against the relevant risk-adjusted global benchmarks; and (b) whether the Government sees the need to review the capital allocation and investment risks framework of GIC, Temasek and MAS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: asked the Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (a) whether the Government is aware if GIC uses risk-adjusted performance metrics such as the Sharpe ratio in assessing portfolio performance relative to its reference portfolio; and (b) if so, whether a description of such metrics can be provided at a high level.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: My reply will also cover Question No 4 for written answer filed by Mr Ng Shi Xuan for today's Sitting.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Such comparisons are often done, but they should be interpreted in their proper context because different funds operate under different mandates and risk profiles.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: The Government assesses GIC and Temasek's performance primarily against their respective mandates and risk profiles, and not with other funds.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Our focus has always been on long-term performance, rather than on short-term or year-to-year fluctuations.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: GIC is the Government's fund manager, and its mandate is to preserve and enhance the international purchasing power of the assets under its management.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: In recent years, GIC took pre-emptive measures to moderate its risk exposure, in anticipation of increased market volatility and heightened valuations.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: These measures were intended to keep portfolio risks within acceptable limits and to guard against the possibility of significant asset impairment in the event of a sharp market correction.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: But as equity markets have continued to remain elevated, these prudent de-risking measures resulted in some foregone returns.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Any assessment of returns must, therefore, be considered alongside the risks that are taken to achieve them – a point that Assoc Prof Jamus Lim made, where he referred to the Sharpe ratio in his Parliamentary Question (PQ).

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: GIC monitors a wide range of risk indicators, including and beyond the Sharpe ratio.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: In fact, GIC publishes both the returns and volatility or the risks associated with its portfolio in its annual report to provide a more complete picture.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Ultimately, what is more important is the longer-term performance that is achieved within acceptable risk limits.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: This outcome reflects, in part, GIC’s active management, which enabled it to consistently add value to portfolio returns, preserve the international purchasing power of the assets under its management and deliver returns above global inflation.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Temasek began as a holding company for the Government’s local assets.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: While Singapore-based Temasek Portfolio Companies (TPCs) continue to form a core part of its total portfolio, Temasek has progressively expanded its direct equity investments overseas – initially in Asia, and more recently, across global markets.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Temasek operates mainly as an active, bottom-up investor.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: It does not operate against a conventional reference portfolio.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Instead, it invests directly in companies in the geographies and domains where it has built deep capabilities, and where it sees long-term growth potential.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Relative to GIC, Temasek therefore operates at the higher end of the risk spectrum.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: In recent years, Temasek’s performance was affected by the performance of the Chinese market, though this was mitigated by higher returns from its growing investments in Europe and the United States (US).

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We will continue to review their mandates and performance regularly, in line with changes in the global economic investment landscape.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Some Members asked about the implications of our investment entities’ recent performance on the sustainability of the Net Investment Returns Contribution (NIRC) and the Government’s ability to meet our Central Provident Fund (CPF) liabilities.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: As explained in this House previously, the Net Investment Return framework was designed to ensure a steady and sustainable stream of income for the annual Budget.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: The Government is able to meet all debt servicing costs and obligations, including the committed CPF rates through the Special Singapore Government Securities (SSGS).

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: GIC does not just manage the SSGS or CPF monies on their own, but a combined pool of Government funds, including a significant sum of unencumbered assets.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: This approach allows GIC to invest for the long term and to secure good long-term returns.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: As investment markets are uncertain and volatile, GIC’s returns over shorter periods could be low or even negative.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: But the Government is able to absorb these short-term market risks, because it has a strong balance sheet.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: This substantial buffer of net assets enables the Government to meet the obligations on its liabilities and continues to underpin the Government’s strong fiscal position.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First of all, I would like to declare that I am an employee of a financial institution.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the previous PQ, we have actually discussed about expenditure on healthcare and others being more demanding.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, my two supplementary questions, Mr Speaker: first, how will the Ministry model the impact of a prolonged global resolve cycle on sovereign investment returns and the resulting implications for the Budget stability and social spending sustainability?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My second supplementary question is whether the Government plans to enhance long-term public reporting on portfolio risks?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think the Acting Minister mentioned the Sharpe ratio and others as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But in terms of public reporting on portfolio risks, volatility and drawdowns for Singapore's foreign investment entities to strengthen public confidence, as reliance on investment income increases?

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: The Government's approach on assessing the returns of our investment entities is to take a long-term view.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Market outcomes will inevitably fluctuate from year to year, there will be periods where returns are weak.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: But the way our system works is that these are not directly linked to our NIRC.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: The Government's strong balance sheet, as I explained earlier in my reply, enables it to take investment risks and ride out market cycles that are inherent in investing for the long term.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We have a significant buffer on net assets, which enables the Government to guarantee CPF savings and pay fair interest rates on CPF savings despite changes in the financial cycle.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And this is also why we are able to have a significant stream of investment income through the NIRC, which is then used to meet important spending priorities, as we discussed earlier.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: So, the impact of a single year, or even a few years' worth of lower returns will take time to be passed through to the NIRC due to the smoothing of the asset base.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Notwithstanding all these, we recognise that it is becoming structurally more difficult or more challenging to generate good investment returns in the current global environment and this trend is likely to persist in the longer term.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Hence, the Government will indeed have to monitor this and take a prudent approach to ensure that our investment income is able to meet our spending and our long-term obligations.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: On the hon Member's question on whether or not the Government intends to enhance long-term public reporting, I think the investment entities already provide quite a good amount of public information on their investment approach and on their returns.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: This can be found in their annual reports, their regular press releases, and occasionally in their opinion and research pieces which they put out.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Temasek, as a direct investor, releases even more information.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: They talk about total portfolio value, its investment approach, the domains and the geographical areas where they are investing.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And I will encourage Members as well as members of the public to look at the information that they put online.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Over time, GIC and Temasek have disclosed more information, and we will continue to encourage them to review if there are other meaningful disclosures to make.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I have two supplementary questions, one on GIC and the other on Temasek.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I understand that GIC has publicly stated that it does not regard its 65/35 Global Equity Bond Reference portfolio as a benchmark, but rather as an expression of risk tolerance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: GIC has also publicly stated that it has attained lower returns, but with lower volatility.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For me, taken together, that suggests that GIC has either taken less risk than what its reference portfolio would suggest, or that it has returned less than what might be expected, given its risk profile.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, my question is whether the Ministry plans to undertake any steps to address the lower returns received by GIC relative to its reference portfolio; or if it is indeed satisfied with this more conservative approach, why does it not request GIC to adopt a different reference portfolio with lower risk?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My second question is on Temasek and I note the Minister's response on how its mandate is more to focus on companies rather than indexes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Nevertheless, I wonder if the Minister would be able to share how Temasek has performed on a risk adjusted basis, relative to the other sovereign wealth fund, GIC?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And if indeed it is taking on such concentrated risk, I also wonder if there is room to reconsider its geographical diversification strategy adopted in the early 2000s and return to a more domestically oriented mandate.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: As I mentioned in my reply earlier, the Government assesses the returns of our investment entities based on their mandates and risk profiles.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: The Member referred to the 65/35 reference portfolio, which is on the GIC website.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: That is not a returns benchmark, but is an expression of our risk tolerance and the risk profile we would like GIC to take.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Ultimately, the Government assesses GIC performance based primarily on whether it has met this mandate.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: There will be periods where GIC takes less risk than the reference portfolio.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And as I mentioned in my earlier reply, GIC did pre-emptively decide to de-risk in periods which had resulted in foregone returns.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Should GIC not have de-risked and ridden through the drawdowns?

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I think that is a matter of a judgement.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: While one can ride through market cycles, there have also been instances where the stocks or the assets are permanently impaired.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And because of the mandate of GIC, it has to balance with the need to preserve our capital assets, I think that is a judgement that they have taken.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: On hindsight, we can always make all sorts of assertions, but they have taken that decision to de-risk and preserve our capital, and still be able to make the returns that we expect of them.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Ultimately, every investment fund must operate according to its own mandate and risk appetite.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We expect GIC to construct its portfolio to both safeguard our assets and to also achieve our returns.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: The approach that they have taken has helped them build a diversified portfolio that is resilient to market cycles and volatility, while achieving good risk adjusted returns.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: On the hon Member's second question on how to assess Temasek's performance, as I mentioned earlier, Temasek is different from GIC.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: It has a history of how it has gotten to where it is today.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: It started off as a holding company for Singapore Temasek-linked portfolio companies.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Over time, it has broadened its coverage to include investments globally.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: It has, in the process of doing so, tried to give a sense of how it is performing on these areas, and on its website, it has referred to a few international indexes, whether it is the MSCI World Index or the Singapore stock market Index when it comes to measuring performance of the local companies.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I think these are possible ways of seeing how they are performing.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We do not intervene in individual investment decisions that are made by Temasek.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: So, which geographies they choose to go into and which domains they prefer to invest in, these are things we leave to the management.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: The Government works with the board to make sure that Temasek meets the mandate that we have set out for them and we do not want to have to intervene in these decisions that they make on individual investments.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: And a Happy New Year to all Parliamentary colleagues, including our Nominated Member of Parliament colleagues.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: With regard to the Senior Minister of State's reply, I fully agree and accept that global rankings of investment returns are not helpful because they do not take into account the unique investment mandates and the unique contexts that each country's investment entity invest in.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: The first question is, when should we worry?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I note the Senior Minister of State's reply, but when should we worry?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: What level of long-term investment returns should be the threshold which triggers a Government review of the NIRC framework to look at its sustainability, based on new structural trends in the global investment climate?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: And the second question is in regard to the fact that GIC and Temasek are active managers that have illiquid portfolios.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: We should expect better returns from active investment managers, as well as a premium from illiquidity.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: That is why the Government will continue to take a prudent approach in ensuring that our investment income is able to meet our long-term obligations.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: But as I have explained earlier, the basis for why we are able to do the things that we are doing today is not because of year-to-year fluctuations in terms of market performance.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And so, in that sense, I think we have to continue to make sure that the mandates of the investment entities continue to be met, that they understand that they are doing this for the longer term, and they are able to take strategies and to take the right decisions to ensure that the returns over the longer term are indeed sustainable.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: As to whether we should be concerned whether the GIC and our investment entities are earning alpha, I think it is quite understandable that we look at how potentially the investment entities performance are benchmarked towards, for example, simple passive global benchmarks.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: When we do not have investment expertise or do not have time to make investments, the most common investment advice is just leave it to the market.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We decide to buy an index fund, let them decide what to do.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: But that is not what we are doing, because GIC here is the Government's fund manager.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: They have a large pool of assets that range from the passive assets to assets that require them to take a closer monitoring and to make sure that those assets continue to generate high returns and they have to make active decisions to manage them.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: If they had not done so, our asset base could have been permanently impaired, as other funds would have experienced during this period.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: So, I think we have to leave the professionals to do the work that they do.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: The Government works with the GIC board to make sure that the mandate continues to be met, given the risk profile of what we want them to do, to take a more conservative approach, to preserve our capital base.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And we think they have met the expectations in this regard.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There are two questions for the Acting Minister.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, can I ask the Acting Minister, whether the Ministry of Finance sees investing more of our Reserves into the local infrastructures that comes with commercial returns, as another way to deploy our growing Reserves?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: My second question is related to what the Acting Minister has said in his reply on Temasek.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: One portfolio is the local companies that they hold.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For strategic reasons, we want to hold these companies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And the other one is the international portfolio, which actually comes with different management investment skills.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And as such, we will have to assess for their difference in performance.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For example, the holding company for the strategic companies that we hold, like Singapore Airlines or PSA and so on, we would not expect Temasek to actively trade this portfolio or choose levels to buy and sell; whereas the international portfolio, there are some investment decisions to be made there, and how they charge the market, how they perform; we want to assess that.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, can I ask that Acting Minister, whether in terms of evaluating the performance of Temasek, would the Ministry consider carving out that local portfolio, that we hold for strategic reasons, to measure the performance separately from the portfolio that is invested internationally?

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Number one, I think is on whether or not, given the competition with global funds, whether Temasek or GIC should take a different focus and to focus on investment in local infrastructure – I think that was the first question.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And the second question, was whether or not, given that it has a cluster, in terms of local Singapore companies, whether we should evaluate performance differently.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I think in gist, those are the two questions.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And so, insofar as requiring them to have a specific investment focus or to invest locally, I think that is something as an entity, they need to decide and in light of the mandate that we have given them, to see whether that it is the most preferred strategy.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: So, we will not direct it personally or directly, but we would leave them to make those decisions.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: As the hon Member said, it started off as a company with deep expertise in managing our local TPCs.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Over time, it is moving towards becoming more of a global investor with more geographical diversification and thus, this also requires Temasek to build up its own capabilities – just as it had built up its capabilities managing the portfolio of Temasek companies.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I think it is a matter of judgement for them to do this, as long as they achieve the mandate that we have given to them.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Bearing in mind also that there are synergies between the different portfolios.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: In managing the local Temasek-linked companies, there are benefits to having a global outlook on matters, having some global expertise and domain expertise in different areas, which I think Temasek is very focused on trying to generate as a result of their investment disposition.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: My second question is how does the Government intend to act under a scenario where GIC's returns consistently underperform SSGS interest rates?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Would it then be sustainable for the Government to continue maintaining the current SSGS interest rates?

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: This enables us to take investment risks and to ride out the market cycles that are inherent in investing for the longer term.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We have a significant buffer of net assets, which enables the Government to guarantee CPF savings and to pay fair interest rates on CPF savings despite market cycles.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: The way this is done is it insulates the CPF returns and interest rates from the vagaries of the market.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I think the Member has asked a question on this previously as well and we can refer to the answer there.
